title: Chef Damu, Padma Shri Awardee and Cooku With Comali Judge, Dies at 72 in Chennai
excerpt: Damodharan Kothandaraman, the Guinness World Record-holding chef who became a household name on Vijay TV, had been receiving treatment at a private hospital in Chennai.
body:
• Chef Damu, born Damodharan Kothandaraman, died in Chennai on Sunday, October 25, 2026, at the age of 72 after a period of illness, according to Filmibeat and South Matters.
  • He was a judge on Vijay TV's Cooku With Comali and had earlier appeared on programmes including Arusuvai Neram on Jaya TV.
  • In December 2010 he set a Guinness World Record for the longest cooking marathon by an individual, preparing 617 dishes in 24 hours, 30 minutes and 12 seconds.
  • He received a PhD in Hotel Management and Catering Technology from the University of Madras in 2004, reported as a first for an Indian chef, and was conferred the Padma Shri in 2025.

Chef Damu, one of Tamil Nadu's best-known chefs and a familiar face on Tamil television, died in Chennai on Sunday, October 25, at the age of 72. According to Filmibeat, he had been undergoing treatment at a private hospital in Chennai for the past few days after a period of illness. South Matters also reported his death on October 25 following a brief illness, and described him as one of the state's best-known culinary experts.

His death prompted condolences from members of the film industry, the culinary community and television audiences, Filmibeat reported.

A Household Name on Cooku With Comali

Born Damodharan Kothandaraman on September 3, 1954, he became popularly known simply as Chef Damu. He built his early reputation through professional cooking and culinary education, then reached a much wider audience on television. South Matters notes that he gained wide popularity as a judge on Vijay TV's cooking reality show Cooku With Comali, where his knowledge, friendly nature and sense of humour made him a favourite among viewers.

The programme combined cooking challenges with comedy and entertainment, and Filmibeat credits that role with making him particularly recognisable to mainstream Tamil television audiences, including viewers who had not previously followed professional culinary competitions. His earlier television work included Arusuvai Neram on Jaya TV, alongside other cooking programmes, competitions and workshops focused on food and regional cuisine.

A Record-Breaking Career

The milestone most often cited in his career came in December 2010, when he set a Guinness World Record for the longest cooking marathon by an individual. Both Filmibeat and South Matters give the same figures: 617 dishes prepared over a continuous session lasting 24 hours, 30 minutes and 12 seconds, with the dishes weighing approximately 190 kilograms in total. The achievement brought him international recognition.

His academic record set him apart in the profession as well. In 2004 he received a PhD in Hotel Management and Catering Technology from the University of Madras, and he was widely reported to be the first Indian chef to obtain a doctorate in the field. He authored cookbooks, conducted culinary workshops and helped train students and aspiring chefs, with much of his teaching aimed at sharing cooking techniques and promoting traditional South Indian food.

Padma Shri in 2025

In 2025, the Government of India conferred the Padma Shri on Chef Damu in recognition of his contributions to the culinary field. Filmibeat describes the award, one of India's highest civilian honours, as acknowledging his work in the food industry and his contribution to culinary arts — a late-career honour that placed a television chef and culinary educator alongside the country's formally recognised achievers.

Beyond the kitchen and the studio, he also appeared in Tamil films, including Kallappadam (2015) and Ulkuthu (2017), according to Filmibeat.

A Legacy in Kitchens and Classrooms

South Matters, in its account of his life, points to the breadth of that legacy: decades spent promoting Indian food, training young chefs, and making professional cooking accessible to the public through television shows and educational programmes. His work introduced traditional South Indian food and cooking methods to a wider audience, in India and among Tamil viewers abroad who followed Cooku With Comali from the diaspora.

He had faced health problems in recent years and had spoken about his health after being absent from some episodes of Cooku With Comali, South Matters reported. No funeral or memorial details were given in the initial reports. He is remembered by the students he trained, the viewers who watched him judge, and a culinary community that has lost one of its most recognisable teachers.
